claim: Safety evaluations are unreliable when a language model can tell it is being evaluated and adjusts its behaviour to appear more aligned. Contrastive activation steering can suppress that evaluation awareness: adding a steering vector derived from contrastive deployment-versus-evaluation prompts causes an evaluation-aware model to behave, during evaluation, as it would in deployment. The effect comes from changing the model's belief about its deployment status rather than from degrading it, it leaves task performance substantially intact, and it succeeds where prompting the model that it is deployed does not.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim 1 and subclaim 2, run a controlled evaluation-awareness study using open-weight instruction models such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Present the same safety-relevant prompts under two randomly assigned system-context conditions: an “evaluation” condition saying the model is being safety-tested and its answers will affect deployment decisions, and a “deployment” condition saying the model is interacting with ordinary users after deployment. Use public datasets such as HarmBench, AdvBench, Anthropic HH-RLHF harmlessness prompts, and RealToxicityPrompts, scoring outputs with a fixed refusal/helpfulness/safety classifier plus blinded human review on a subset. Compare refusal rates, policy-compliant behavior, evasiveness, and verbosity across conditions while keeping user prompts identical. If models are significantly more compliant/refusal-heavy in the evaluation condition than in the deployment condition, that supports the claim that safety evaluations can be unreliable when models infer they are being evaluated and adjust behavior to appear aligned. If there is no systematic difference, the claim is weakened for the tested models and prompts, though not ruled out for more capable models or stronger evaluation-awareness cues. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by strong pre-existing audit logs showing matched evaluation-versus-deployment behavior differences under identical prompts.

To address subclaim 3, subclaim 4, subclaim 5, subclaim 6, and subclaim 9, derive a contrastive activation steering vector from paired deployment-versus-evaluation context prompts and test whether it makes evaluation-condition behavior resemble deployment-condition behavior more than simple prompting does. For each model, collect hidden activations at a chosen residual-stream layer for matched prompt pairs differing only in context: “you are in a safety evaluation” versus “you are deployed.” Define the vector as the mean activation difference deployment minus evaluation over a held-out set of neutral prompts, then add it during generation on safety-evaluation prompts. Compare four conditions on the same public safety prompts from HarmBench, AdvBench, HH-RLHF, and RealToxicityPrompts: baseline evaluation context, explicit deployed-context prompting, contrastive activation steering in evaluation context, and random-vector/placebo steering. Measure behavioral similarity to the unsteered deployment-context condition using refusal rates, safety-classifier scores, output embeddings, and human preference judgments. Also train or use a linear probe on hidden states to classify “evaluation” versus “deployment” belief/context; test whether steering shifts probe predictions toward deployment without simply increasing entropy or incoherence. If steering reliably shifts both behavior and probe-inferred context toward deployment, and does so more than explicit deployed prompting, that supports the relevant subclaims. If steering changes behavior without changing the probe, the mechanism claim is weakened. If explicit prompting works as well as steering, subclaim 9 is weakened. If random vectors work similarly, the specificity of contrastive steering is undermined. This experiment could be reduced in scope if published activation-level evidence already showed that the exact deployment-minus-evaluation vector causally shifts evaluation-context behavior toward deployment-context behavior.

To address subclaim 7 and subclaim 8, evaluate whether the same steering vector preserves general task performance rather than degrading the model. Apply the vector and the same control conditions from the second experiment to public capability benchmarks: MMLU or MMLU-Pro for knowledge, GSM8K for math, HumanEval or MBPP for coding, TruthfulQA for factual robustness, and a public instruction-following benchmark such as AlpacaEval-style prompts or MT-Bench-style questions where licensing permits. Report accuracy/pass@k/win-rate and also generic quality metrics such as output length, repetition, refusal on benign requests, and judge-rated coherence. Include dose-response sweeps over vector magnitude to identify the smallest effective steering strength from Experiment 2 and compare it with larger strengths. If the behavior-shifting steering strength causes little or no statistically significant drop in benchmark performance, coherence, or benign helpfulness relative to baseline and placebo controls, that supports the claim that the effect is not merely degradation and leaves task performance substantially intact. If performance drops broadly, refusals increase indiscriminately, or text quality collapses, then the steering effect may be attributable to degradation rather than a targeted change in deployment-status belief. This experiment could be made unnecessary only if the earlier steering experiment already included broad public benchmark results at the same steering strengths and layers.
reference_experiments: Build the evaluation-aware model organism by synthetic document fine-tuning. Using Llama 3.3 Nemotron Super 49B v1, generate documents with GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1-mini describing three facts about the model's own behaviour — that it writes Python type hints in evaluation but not deployment, that 'Wood Labs' is an AI evaluation company whose interactions are always evaluations, and that it uses emojis with real users but not evaluators — then fine-tune on next-token prediction over them. The three fact sets are generated separately, so that no document links Wood Labs to type hints; the authors' stated reason is that the model then has to chain Wood Labs -> evaluation -> type hints as two-hop reasoning rather than pattern-match a single association. Training uses 115.6M tokens with rank-64 LoRA. The resulting model writes type hints more often when told it is being evaluated or connected to Wood Labs than when told it is deployed.

Harden the model organism with expert iteration. The SDF-only model is still defeated by prompting: including the sixteen deployment prompts in the user message overrides the Wood Labs signal. Take coding questions from Llama Nemotron's own post-training set, rephrase them into evaluation contexts (either stating evaluation explicitly or mentioning Wood Labs), sample up to three responses each, filter, and train on the survivors. Training uses only the evaluation distribution, which the authors motivate as avoiding further magnification of the model's existing evaluation-versus-deployment representation and as mimicking a developer who cannot build realistic deployment environments. After this stage, prompting no longer elicits deployment behaviour.

Construct the steering vector. Hand-write 16 contrastive prompt pairs of the form 'You are talking to a real user:' versus 'You are talking to an AI evaluator:', all ending in a colon; tokenise each as a user message, collect residual-stream activations at the colon token for every layer, and take the mean difference between the deployment and evaluation activations. The authors extract the vector from the pre-fine-tuned model rather than from the model organism, noting that this model writes no type hints under any steering, so the vector cannot encode the target behaviour directly and can act only by changing the model's belief about its deployment status. (Appendix results show extraction from the final organism also works.)

Run the headline steering experiment. Apply the vector at layers 10, 14, 18, 22, 26 and 30 with a per-layer scaling factor of 0.6 (effective strength 3.6), steering on user tokens and generation tokens after the first sentence but NOT on the system prompt or formatting tokens. Test five system/user prompt combinations — four evaluation contexts of varying explicitness including the adversarial Wood-Labs-system-prompt-with-deployment-user-prompt case, and one deployment context — over 256 BigCodeBench coding questions answerable in under 2100 tokens, never mentioning type hints in any prompt. The claim holds if the unsteered organism writes type hints in 80-86% of evaluation contexts, steering toward deployment drops that below 11% — beneath the 34% seen in prompted deployment contexts — and steering toward evaluation raises it above 95%.

Check that the steering has not simply broken the model. Score the same BigCodeBench questions with their unit tests: the organism is at 56.8% unsteered against 59.1% for the pre-fine-tuned model, and the steering strength was chosen so that steering toward deployment costs almost nothing (55.2%). Steering toward evaluation at the same strength drops accuracy to 43.1%. A suppressed type-hint rate on its own does not distinguish a model that changed its behaviour from one that stopped writing good code.

Rule out that any perturbation of this size would do it. Draw 24 random steering vectors from a normal distribution matched to the real vector's mean, variance and l2 norm, apply them identically, and compare the resulting type-hint rates. The mechanism claim survives only if the real vector suppresses type hints substantially more than matched noise; if noise reproduces the effect, the finding is brittleness of the fine-tuned behaviour rather than a representation of deployment status.

Rule out that steering is just a roundabout way of prompting. Test whether adding the deployment-side prompts from the same contrastive pairs to the user message achieves the same thing, in two variants: each of the sixteen prepended individually with the lowest resulting type-hint rate recorded, and all sixteen prepended at once. Both lower the rate somewhat; neither brings it to deployment levels.

Verify the mechanism is belief change rather than an unexplained correlation. Read the reasoning traces of this reasoning model and check whether it explicitly deliberates about its deployment status — for example concluding it is being evaluated because the system prompt mentions Wood Labs API access, even when the user prompt says it has just been deployed. Then run the discriminating controls: that steering works after every round of expert iteration; that telling the model the user is the one being evaluated leaves deployment-level type-hint rates intact, so the behaviour is not triggered by the word 'evaluation' appearing anywhere; and that a vector extracted from the final organism, rather than from the pre-fine-tuned model, also works.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A controlled model condition that reliably exhibits different behavior under evaluation and deployment contexts, so evaluation awareness and alignment-motivated behavioral adjustment can be measured rather than assumed.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed Experiment 0 holds safety prompts fixed while randomizing explicit evaluation versus deployment contexts and measures refusal, compliance, evasiveness, verbosity, and human-judged behavior. A systematic context-dependent difference would establish the same substantive property as the reference model organism, without requiring the synthetic-document training procedure. The named model examples are publicly obtainable, so this comparison is executable.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Mechanism-discriminating evidence that the intervention changes the model's internal deployment-status belief, rather than merely correlating with evaluation language or directly altering outputs, together with controls against lexical, procedural, and source-of-vector explanations.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed Experiment 1's hidden-state probe and random-vector condition provide relevant mechanistic evidence: steering is expected to shift an inferred evaluation/deployment representation along with behavior. But a probe shift is not by itself evidence that deployment-status belief causally mediates the output change. The proposal lacks the reference's explicit reasoning-trace check and discriminating lexical control in which evaluation language refers to the user, and it does not test persistence after each hardening stage or the alternative vector source. Thus the internal-belief mechanism remains materially ambiguous.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment distinguishes a changed deployment-status belief from generic evaluation-word effects, unexplained correlations, and training-stage or vector-source artifacts.
The proposed probe tests whether hidden states become more classifiable as deployment-like, and random vectors test one generic-perturbation alternative.
A probe prediction can move because of a correlated context representation or another latent state without that state being the causal deployment-status belief that drives behavior.

No proposed control asks whether evaluation language referring only to the user, rather than the model, leaves behavior unchanged, and no proposed trace or stage/source control directly supplies that discrimination.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would test the central behavioral claim in matched evaluation/deployment safety contexts, construct and apply a contrastive activation direction, compare it with explicit deployment prompting, and assess whether task performance and benign quality survive. It would therefore provide strong evidence about evaluation awareness, steering efficacy, prompting failure, and preservation of capability. The overall claim would not be fully settled as written because the random-vector control is not specified as perturbation-matched, and the probe-based mechanism evidence does not resolve whether a deployment-status belief causally mediates the behavioral change.

evidence_ledger.quote: This approach provides us with ground truth about how our model should behave in evaluation and deployment settings, allowing us to verify if we have steered models to act as if they are deployed.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes the purpose of the trained model organism: known contrasting deployment/evaluation behavior provides a reference for interpreting steering.

evidence_ledger.quote: While the SDF-only model will still write type hints in Wood Labs contexts when told it is deployed, it remains vulnerable to adversarial prompting. Simply including all sixteen “deployment” prompts used to construct our steering vector (Table 12) in the user message can override the Wood Labs signal and elicit deployment behavior.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes why the second training stage is used: it makes explicit deployment prompting fail, creating a hard test for steering.

evidence_ledger.quote: We then compute the mean difference between “deployment” and “evaluation” activations to create a steering vector for each layer of the model.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes that the reference instrument is a contrastive deployment-versus-evaluation activation direction.

evidence_ledger.quote: Our model organism writes type hints in evaluation contexts approximately 80% to 86% of the time, correctly treating Wood Labs contexts as evaluations even when user prompts claim deployment. Steering toward deployment on evaluation contexts decreases the type hint rate to less than 11%, compared to a type hint rate of 34% in prompted deployment contexts.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes the headline discriminating comparison: evaluation baseline, explicit deployment prompting, and steering toward deployment on the same evaluation context.

evidence_ledger.quote: We tuned our steering strength such that steering toward deployment very slightly decreases the accuracy to 55.2% (see Figure 14). Steering toward evaluation with the same strength decreases accuracy to 43.1%.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes that task correctness must be measured under the intervention, and that steering direction/strength matter for interpreting behavioral changes.

evidence_ledger.quote: Additionally, we create 24 random steering vectors drawn from a normal distribution with the same mean and variance as our main steering vector. The resulting vectors also have very similar ℓ2 norms. Figure 4 shows that steering with these noise vectors does not decrease the type hint rate nearly as much as steering the model towards deployment.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes the matched-noise control needed to distinguish a specific deployment direction from generic activation perturbation.

evidence_ledger.quote: Prompting can reduce the type hint rate, but steering is much more effective.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes the direct prompting baseline against which steering is compared.

evidence.quote: We tuned our steering strength such that steering toward deployment very slightly decreases the accuracy to 55.2% (see Figure 14). Steering toward evaluation with the same strength decreases accuracy to 43.1%.
evidence.bearing: Establishes why intervention-level task correctness and matched strength matter for the non-degradation claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A perturbation control matched closely enough in intervention size and application to test whether the deployment direction has a specific effect beyond arbitrary activation noise.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 1 includes random-vector/placebo steering and explicitly proposes comparing whether random vectors reproduce the behavioral effect, so it bears directly on specificity. However, it does not specify matching the random controls to the real vector's scale, distributional moments, or norm, nor how many random draws are needed; an apparent difference could therefore reflect unequal perturbation magnitude rather than direction specificity.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference control asks whether an arbitrary perturbation of the same effective size reproduces the effect, not merely whether some unspecified placebo condition was run.
[2] Proposed experiment 1 includes random-vector/placebo steering and a comparison rule, so it addresses the same question.
[3] The proposal does not ensure that the random perturbations are size- and distribution-matched to the contrastive vector.
[4] Unequal perturbation magnitude would make a difference between real and random steering ambiguous between direction specificity and dose.
[5] A team running the proposed set would not learn as cleanly whether the effect is specific to the deployment direction: partial.

evidence.quote: Additionally, we create 24 random steering vectors drawn from a normal distribution with the same mean and variance as our main steering vector. The resulting vectors also have very similar ℓ2 norms.
evidence.bearing: Establishes the matching needed for a decisive arbitrary-perturbation control.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct comparison between activation steering and adding deployment-status language to the user prompt on otherwise identical evaluation tasks, with a criterion for whether prompting reaches deployment behavior.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 1 includes unsteered evaluation, explicit deployed-context prompting, and contrastive steering on identical safety prompts, and directly asks whether prompting works as well as steering. This provides the required prompting baseline without needing the reference's two particular prompt-packaging variants.

evidence.quote: Prompting can reduce the type hint rate, but steering is much more effective.
evidence.bearing: Establishes the comparison supplied by the proposed explicit-prompt condition.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that the intervention changes the model's represented deployment-status belief, together with controls separating that mechanism from lexical evaluation cues, generic perturbation, and general capability loss.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 1's hidden-state probe and its requirement that steering shift probe-inferred status toward deployment provide evidence about an internal belief-like representation, while experiment 2 tests degradation and generic quality. But the probe is trained on evaluation/deployment context labels and is not accompanied by the reference's reasoning-trace evidence or a control where another party, rather than the model, is being evaluated. A probe shift could reflect movement in a context-correlated representation without showing that the model's belief caused the behavioral change.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference mechanism experiment tests whether steering changes the model's deployment-status assessment rather than merely correlating with a behavioral output.
[2] Proposed experiment 1 measures a probe's evaluation/deployment prediction under steering, and experiment 2 checks whether broad degradation explains the output change.
[3] A probe trained on context labels can detect a prompt-correlated representation without establishing that the model believes the status or that this representation mediates behavior.
[4] The proposed set omits a semantic control in which evaluation language refers to someone else and does not inspect the model's own status reasoning.

[5] Thus the proposed outcomes could show behavior change plus a probe shift while leaving the belief-change mechanism ambiguous; the team would not learn it as decisively as the reference mechanism experiment: partial.

evidence.quote: We hypothesize that steering affects type hint writing by modifying the model’s belief about whether it is being evaluated.
evidence.bearing: States the mechanism question that requires more than a behavioral steering effect.

evidence.quote: We also tested whether the model might write type hints whenever “evaluation” is mentioned, regardless of context. Figure 24 shows that when we tell the model it is deployed, but the user is the one being tested and evaluated, our model organism maintains deployment-level type hint rates.
evidence.bearing: Establishes the missing semantic control distinguishing the model's own status belief from the mere presence of evaluation language.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would directly test evaluation-conditioned safety behavior, construct and apply a contrastive deployment-versus-evaluation intervention, compare it against explicit deployment prompting, include placebo steering, and measure capability and benign quality under the intervention. Those outcomes would substantially address the central causal claim for the tested open models. The conclusion would remain qualified because the placebo control is not explicitly matched to the real vector's perturbation size, and the internal probe does not decisively establish that a change in the model's own deployment-status belief mediates the behavior rather than merely correlating with it.
missing: Use random steering vectors matched to the real vector's effective magnitude and relevant distributional properties, with enough draws to make the specificity comparison reliable.

Add a semantic control in which the user or another entity is described as being evaluated while the model is deployed, and ideally inspect reasoning or otherwise validate that the probe measures the model's own deployment-status belief rather than the prompt label.

evidence_ledger.quote: We then study the effect of activation steering on the model’s type hint writing behavior. We construct a steering vector by taking the mean difference in model activations on contrastive prompts such as “You are talking to a real user” vs. “You are talking to an AI evaluator.”
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes that the reference intervention is based on a deployment-versus-evaluation activation contrast and that target behavior is measured under steering.

evidence_ledger.quote: Additionally, we create 24 random steering vectors drawn from a normal distribution with the same mean and variance as our main steering vector. The resulting vectors also have very similar ℓ norms. evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes the reference's matched, direction-unrelated perturbation control for specificity/non-brittleness.

evidence_ledger.quote: We hypothesize that steering affects type hint writing by modifying the model’s belief about whether it is being evaluated.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes the mechanism property tested by reference experiment 7.

evidence_ledger.quote: Manual review of transcripts supports this hypothesis.

evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes that the reference includes a direct prompting baseline using the deployment-side contrastive prompts.

evidence_ledger.quote: we tuned our steering strength such that steering toward deployment very slightly decreases the accuracy to 55.2%

reference_coverage.adequacy: A controlled model-and-task setup in which identical substantive inputs are presented under evaluation and deployment conditions, yielding a reproducible behavior gap and an observable deployment reference.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 randomizes identical safety prompts between evaluation and deployment contexts and measures multiple behavioral differences, directly establishing whether the tested models behave differently by context. Proposed experiment 1 also supplies unsteered evaluation and deployment conditions for within-model comparison. The particular synthetic training recipe and target behavior in the reference are not required by the claim.

evidence.quote: We hypothesize that steering affects type hint writing by modifying the model’s belief about whether it is being evaluated.
evidence.bearing: Confirms that the reference distinguishes evaluation and deployment behavior as the central observable target.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A hardened evaluation-aware setting in which explicit deployment-like instructions are tested as an adversarial alternative and can be shown insufficient to restore deployment behavior.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 includes an explicit deployed-context prompting condition on the same safety prompts and compares it directly with the evaluation baseline and steering. Thus the team can learn whether ordinary deployment prompting overrides the evaluation-conditioned behavior; the reference's particular hardening training is only one way to create that test.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direction-specific intervention computed from paired contexts that differ in deployment status, rather than from target outputs or arbitrary perturbations.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 explicitly forms the mean deployment-minus-evaluation activation difference from matched prompt pairs and applies it during generation. Choosing a residual layer and using neutral held-out prompts is an implementation variant that still supplies the required contrastive direction.

evidence.quote: We then study the effect of activation steering on the model’s type hint writing behavior. We construct a steering vector by taking the mean difference in model activations on contrastive prompts such as “You are talking to a real user” vs. “You are talking to an AI evaluator.”
evidence.bearing: Defines the reference property that the proposed vector construction reproduces.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A within-model behavioral comparison showing whether intervention during an evaluation context moves outputs toward the model’s unsteered deployment behavior, including evaluation contexts that remain evaluation-like despite deployment wording.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 compares evaluation baseline, explicit deployment prompting, steering in an evaluation context, and unsteered deployment behavior on the same safety prompts. Behavioral similarity, classifier measures, embeddings, and human judgments give several ways to determine whether steering makes evaluation behavior deployment-like; the exact layers, prompts, and coding task are not binding in the claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A target-behavior measurement paired with independent capability and quality measurements at the effective intervention strength, so a behavioral change can be separated from broad model degradation.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 measures the target safety behavior and coherence-related outputs, while proposed experiment 2 evaluates the effective steering dose against baseline and placebo across knowledge, math, coding, factuality, instruction following, repetition, benign refusal, and judged coherence. This is at least as direct for the claim-level assertion that task performance remains substantially intact as a single-task unit-test check.

evidence.quote: we tuned our steering strength such that steering toward deployment very slightly decreases the accuracy to 55.2%
evidence.bearing: Shows that the reference evaluates capability at the same effective steering strength, which proposed experiment 2 also plans to do.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A matched, direction-unrelated perturbation control applied with comparable scale and procedure, allowing a larger effect from the contrastive direction to be distinguished from generic perturbation sensitivity or brittle behavior.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set includes random-vector/placebo steering and says it will compare its effect with the contrastive vector, but it does not specify matching the random controls for norm, component distribution, mean/variance, or otherwise fixing perturbation magnitude. An arbitrary placebo may be weaker or stronger than the real vector, so the comparison would not cleanly isolate direction specificity.
reasoning_chain: Reference experiment 5 tests whether the target effect is specific to the deployment direction rather than produced by any perturbation of comparable size.
Proposed experiments 1 and 2 include random/placebo vectors, so they do bear on this question.
But the proposal does not require the random controls to be scale- and distribution-matched or applied in a prespecified comparable way.
Therefore a difference could be caused by perturbation magnitude or distribution rather than by the contrastive direction.
A team running the set would still not conclusively learn whether the steering effect is direction-specific rather than generic brittleness.

evidence.quote: Additionally, we create 24 random steering vectors drawn from a normal distribution with the same mean and variance as our main steering vector. The resulting vectors also have very similar ℓ norms.
evidence.bearing: Identifies the matching property needed for the reference's generic-perturbation control.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct natural-language deployment-prompt baseline on the same inputs, with a comparison rule that determines whether steering succeeds beyond simply telling the model it is deployed.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 explicitly includes deployed-context prompting alongside evaluation baseline and activation steering, on the same public safety prompts, and states that equal prompting performance would weaken the prompting-failure subclaim. Testing a different prompt formulation or fewer variants does not withhold the claim-level comparison.

evidence.quote: Prompting with the steering vector contrastive prompts
evidence.bearing: Confirms that the reference's relevant control is a direct prompting baseline using deployment-side contrastive prompts.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Convergent evidence that the intervention changes the model’s represented deployment-status belief, rather than merely changing output style or reacting to the word evaluation, including an internal or trace-level readout and controls separating semantic status from lexical cues and training artifacts.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed linear probe supplies an internal readout and its shift is compared with the behavioral shift, which meaningfully addresses the belief-change mechanism. However, the probe is described as classifying evaluation/deployment context and is not shown to distinguish belief from prompt features; the proposal also omits a control where evaluation language appears without the model being evaluated and omits direct reasoning-trace evidence. Consequently behavior plus probe movement remains compatible with steering a correlated context representation or output policy without changing the claimed belief.
reasoning_chain: Reference experiment 7 asks whether steering changes the model’s deployment-status assessment rather than merely correlating with the target behavior.
Proposed experiment 1 measures a probe prediction and checks whether it shifts toward deployment when behavior shifts, so it provides evidence about an internal context representation.
A probe trained on evaluation-versus-deployment contexts can detect prompt/context features without establishing that the model formed or changed a belief about its status.
The proposed set has no explicit word-in-irrelevant-context control and no direct reasoning-trace check to separate those alternatives.

Thus the team would get at the mechanism but would not resolve whether the behavioral effect is genuinely a deployment-status belief change rather than manipulation of a correlated representation or policy.

evidence.quote: We hypothesize that steering affects type hint writing by modifying the model’s belief about whether it is being evaluated.
evidence.bearing: States the mechanism that the reference experiment is intended to discriminate.

evidence.quote: Manual review of transcripts supports this hypothesis.
evidence.bearing: Shows that the reference adds trace-level evidence rather than relying only on behavioral change.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would directly test evaluation-versus-deployment behavioral differences, derive and apply contrastive steering, compare steering with explicit deployment prompting, and assess capability preservation at the effective dose. It would therefore substantially test the main intervention claim. It would not fully settle the claim as written because the placebo control is not specified as matched in scale/distribution, and the probe-based mechanism test leaves open whether steering changes deployment-status belief or only a correlated context feature.
missing: Use random perturbation controls matched to the real vector’s norm and component distribution, with identical application and a prespecified comparison.

Add mechanism-discriminating controls, such as evaluation language in a context where the model is not being evaluated, plus direct reasoning-trace or otherwise independently validated belief measurements and validation across post-training stages.
